newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Low claims boost Allianz domestic profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Low claims boost Allianz domestic profits.

text.p: German insurance giant Allianz AG Holding on Tuesday reported a surge in profits at its domestic non-life unit in 1996, as claims sank to a post-war low and the company continued to sift its books for bad risks.

But at the same time, price pressures in the newly deregulated market and the slack economy weighed on sales, forcing the company to report its first ever fall in domestic premium income in the post-war period.

Allianz Versicherungs AG, which controls the non-life business of the group's soon-to-be-merged eastern and western activities, reported a 41 percent jump in pre-tax earnings to 1.6 billion marks ($955.5 million), although premiums dropped 1.4 percent.
Unit chairman Reiner Hagemann told a news conference that the outlook for business growth this year remained gloomy, but he still expected 1997 to be a "good year" for profits.

"We are reckoning with continued weak growth in the market for 1997, caused by stagnant net income -- in the best case scenario -- as well as a very weak economy and ongoing price pressures," Hagemann said.

The 1996 profit rise -- which is still based on preliminary figures -- came amid a tripling of underwriting profits to 403 million marks and a 16 percent rise in the non-underwriting result, which reached 1.2 billion marks.

Non-underwriting results, which largely comprise investment earnings, were boosted by higher investments, last year's capital markets boom and sell-offs in the unit's fixed income portfolio which generated some 420 million marks.
Meanwhile, tight risk control and a sharp fall in claims -- with drops as high as 20 percent in car theft cases -- helped compensate for price pressures and boost underwriting profit.
Hagemann said total claims dropped by seven percent to 3.7 million instances in 1996 and claims paid fell four percent to 9.4 billion marks.
"God was on our side," Hagemann said, noting that the company was last year largely spared exposure to major disasters, such as those caused by storms or fires.
However, domestic motor insurance premium income dropped 5.4 percent in 1996 to 7.2 billion marks, the main reason for a drop in overall premiums to 17.1 billion marks.

Price pressures, exacerbated in Germany by recent deregulation, have been most evident in the vital car insurance sector where insurers have been forced to introduce more differentiated and cheaper pricing options.

Allianz said it would continue to offer new pricing models for motor insurance. It attracted 40,000 new risks in this sector over the year, bringing total new third-party cover sales up sightly to 850,000 policies.
Looking ahead, Hagemann said the moderate claims trend had continued in early 1997, although claims paid rose five percent in January due to customary winter weather-driven factors.
The integration of the non-life business of Vereinte Versicherungs AG, which Allianz took over in full last year, would also be a major priority.
Allianz plans to close most Vereinte offices which overlap with those of Allianz and harmonise pricing structures between the two companies. Electronic systems are to be harmonised by the year 2000.

Finally, Hagemann called on Bonn to clarify the current debate about tax reform, which includes proposals for a 10 percent tax on certain life insurance benefits -- a move he said would be counter-productive given the need for alternatives to the state pension system.
Allianz staff were fielding 1,500 calls daily on this subject from worried customers, Hagemann said.
